The answer lies in a convergence of structural vulnerabilities. DRC borders nine countries, and cross-border movement allows pathogens to outpace chronically underfunded local surveillance systems. Decades of armed conflict have displaced millions in the affected areas, leaving health facilities damaged and surveillance unable to distinguish Ebola from endemic febrile illness.3 Deforestation and agricultural expansion bring human populations into direct contact with the fruit bat species identified as the principal reservoir hosts for Ebola virus. Hunting and handling of bats as a protein source has been directly implicated in spillover events.45 Beneath these structural conditions lies a deeper vulnerability that epidemiological models consistently underestimate—the erosion of community trust in outside medical responders. Four days after WHO sounded the alarm, residents in Rwampara, Ituri, stormed an Ebola treatment facility and set it alight when authorities refused to release the body of a man who had died there. A day later, a tent at a Médecins Sans Frontières facility in nearby Mongbwalu was also burned.6 These were not isolated acts, nor were they justified. They were warning signs: the latest expression of a pattern throughout DRC’s long history of the disease in which communities, having learned to regard outside health responses with suspicion, signalled the collapse of legitimacy through the most visible means available to them. During the 2018 to 2020 outbreak, WHO documented approximately 390 attacks on health facilities: 11 health workers were killed and 83 were injured.7 A single phrase captured the sentiment across affected communities: “Ebola is a business.”8 This mistrust is not irrational, nor is it misinformation to be corrected with better messaging, though explaining its roots is not the same as excusing violence against health workers. It is a structured disposition rooted in history: colonial medicine that subjected central African populations to forced biomedical campaigns, a legacy that measurably reduces vaccination uptake and trust in medicine today;9 decades of state violence and institutional failure; and more recent Ebola responses that deployed security forces, imposed burial restrictions that disrupted community norms, and excluded local communities from recruitment as health workers and responders in ways that deepened the atmosphere of mistrust.8 When responders later announced experimental vaccines, communities whose trust had already been forfeited were alienated rather than reassured.8 Surveys confirmed that low institutional trust was among the strongest independent predictors of vaccine refusal and delayed care seeking.10 The distinction between community engagement and community ownership matters here. Engagement means communicating strategies designed by international organisations and central government agencies. Ownership means communities participating from the outset: controlling the pace of interventions, deciding on burial practices that respect both necessity and dignity, and having historical grievances treated as legitimate. This is harder and slower than deploying a response team with megaphones, but it is the approach most consistently associated with improved acceptance of public health measures and more effective outbreak control.78 Although vaccines, surveillance, and clinical care were indispensable, sustained community dialogue and increasing reliance on trusted local actors were equally critical to achieving control of the 2018 to 2020 outbreak. Breaking DRC’s cycle of Ebola outbreaks requires investment at two levels. In the current outbreak, these failures are already visible: burial teams have been attacked, patients have fled treatment centres, and frontline responders report that community members question whether the disease is real.11 In the short term, community trust must be treated not as a communication problem but as an operational prerequisite. Local health workers, traditional leaders, and religious figures must lead engagement rather than deliver externally designed messages; burial protocols must be negotiated, not imposed; and feedback mechanisms must let response strategy adapt in real time.7 Longer term, DRC and partners must invest in infrastructure that earns trust before the next outbreak, including functional health facilities, community rooted health workers, and water and sanitation foundations.34 Seventeen outbreaks in 50 years is not a run of bad luck. It is the predictable consequence of structural conditions that have not been addressed with the depth or durability the problem demands. This outbreak is a chance, again, to address them differently, and to finally break the pattern. title_original: How a legacy of mistrust in DRC has led to 17 Ebola outbreaks in 50 years

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addresses why the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has experienced 17 Ebola outbreaks in 50 years, focusing on the structural vulnerabilities and historical mistrust that perpetuate the cycle of disease recurrence. The objective is to understand why DRC faces Ebola repeatedly and what will finally break that cycle.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study is a descriptive analysis of the epidemiological and social context of Ebola outbreaks in DRC, examining the recurrence of outbreaks in the same fragile settings over a 50-year period. It focuses on the structural conditions, community trust, and historical factors contributing to the persistence of Ebola in the region.
analysis.methods: The analysis synthesizes data from WHO reports, epidemiological models, historical records, and surveys to examine the convergence of structural vulnerabilities, including armed conflict, deforestation, and the erosion of community trust. It contrasts community engagement with community ownership to understand the impact on health responses.
analysis.main_results: As of 8 July, 1759 suspected cases and 600 deaths had been reported across the provinces of Ituri and Nord-Kivu, with the Bundibugyo virus disease re-emerging and spreading to Uganda. During the 2018 to 2020 outbreak, WHO documented approximately 390 attacks on health facilities, including 11 health worker deaths and 83 injuries.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret the findings as evidence that mistrust is a structured disposition rooted in history, including colonial medicine, state violence, and exclusionary response strategies. The novelty lies in highlighting the distinction between community engagement and ownership as critical factors in breaking the cycle of mistrust and recurrence.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that addressing structural vulnerabilities and rebuilding community trust are essential for effective Ebola surveillance, prevention, and response. The study implies that global health institutions must prioritize trust-building investments over emergency response to finally end the cycle of outbreaks.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study relies on secondary data and historical records, which may introduce bias and limit generalizability. The evidence strength is moderate due to the descriptive nature of the analysis and the absence of primary research data.

analysis.summary_en: This analysis explores why the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has experienced 17 Ebola outbreaks in 50 years, attributing the recurrence to structural vulnerabilities, including armed conflict, deforestation, and the erosion of community trust. The study highlights historical factors such as colonial medicine, state violence, and exclusionary response strategies that have fostered deep-seated mistrust. As of 8 July, 1759 suspected cases and 600 deaths were reported in the Ituri and Nord-Kivu provinces, with the Bundibugyo virus spreading to Uganda. During the 2018-2020 outbreak, 390 attacks on health facilities occurred, including 11 deaths and 83 injuries among health workers. The authors argue that mistrust is a structured disposition rooted in history and that distinguishing between community engagement and ownership is critical for breaking the cycle of mistrust and recurrence. The study implies that global health institutions must prioritize trust-building investments over emergency response to effectively prevent future outbreaks.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究探讨了刚果民主共和国 (DRC) 在 50 年内经历 17 次埃博拉病毒 暴发 的原因,重点关注导致疾病复发循环的结构性脆弱性和历史不信任。目的是了解刚果民主共和国为何反复面临埃博拉病毒以及什么将最终打破这一循环。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究对刚果民主共和国埃博拉 暴发 的流行病学和社会背景进行了描述性分析,考察了 50 年来 暴发 在相同脆弱环境中的复发情况。它重点关注导致埃博拉病毒在该地区持续存在的结构条件、社区信任和历史因素。
elements_zh.methods: 该分析综合了来自世卫组织报告、流行病学模型、历史记录和调查的数据,以检验结构性脆弱性的趋同性,包括武装冲突、森林砍伐和社区信任的侵蚀。它将社区参与与社区所有权进行对比,以了解对健康应对措施的影响。
elements_zh.main_results: 截至 7 月 8 日,伊图里省和北基伍省报告了 1759 例疑似病例和 600 例死亡,本迪布焦病毒病重新出现并蔓延到乌干达。在 2018 年至 2020 年 暴发 期间,世卫组织记录了大约 390 起针对卫生设施的袭击事件,其中包括 11 名卫生工作者死亡和 83 人受伤。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将这些发现解释为证据,表明不信任是一种植根于历史的结构化倾向,包括殖民医学、国家暴力和排他性应对策略。新颖之处在于强调社区参与和所有权之间的区别,作为打破不信任和复发循环的关键因素。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,解决结构性脆弱性和重建社区信任对于有效预防和应对埃博拉病毒至关重要。该研究表明,全球卫生机构必须优先考虑建立信任投资而不是应急响应,以最终结束 暴发 循环。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究依赖于二手数据和历史记录,这可能会引入偏差并限制普遍性。由于分析的描述性和缺乏主要研究数据,证据强度中等。
